Who is left ... that saw ... first glory--</hi>Many elders present at the laying of the foundation of the second temple who had seen the first temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.13">13</reference>) in all its glory, wept at the contrast presented by the rough and unpromising appearance of the former in its beginnings. From the destruction of the first temple to the second year of Darius Hystaspes, the date of Haggai's prophecy, was a space of seventy years (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>); and to the first year of Cyrus, or the end of the captivity, fifty-two years; so that the elders might easily remember the first temple. The Jews note five points of inferiority: The absence from the second temple of (1) the sacred fire; (2) the Shekinah; (3) the ark and cherubim; (4) the Urim and Thummim; (5) the spirit of prophecy. The connection of it with Messiah more than counterbalanced all these; for He is the antitype to all the five (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how do ye see it now?--</hi>God's estimate of things is very different from man's (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.6">Zec 8:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>). However low their estimate of the present temple ("it") from its outward inferiority, God holds it superior (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zec 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>). <div eID="gen24369" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12992"/><div sID="gen24374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12992"/><hi type="bold">6. Yet once, it is a little while--</hi>or, "(it is) yet a little while." The Hebrew for "once" expresses the indefinite article "a" [Maurer]. Or, "it is yet only a little while"; literally, "one little," that is, a single brief space till a series of movements is to begin; namely, the shakings of nations soon to begin which are to end in the advent of Messiah, "the desire of all nations" [Moore]. The shaking of nations implies judgments of wrath on the foes of God's people, to precede the reign of the Prince of peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.13">Is 13:13</reference>). The kingdoms of the world are but the scaffolding for God's spiritual temple, to be thrown down when their purpose is accomplished. The transitoriness of all that is earthly should lead men to seek "peace" in Messiah's everlasting kingdom (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">He 12:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">28</reference>) [Moore]. The Jews in Haggai's times hesitated about going forward with the work, through dread of the world power, Medo-Persia, influenced by the craft of Samaria. The prophet assures them this and all other world powers are to fall before Messiah, who is to be associated with this temple; therefore they need fear naught. So <reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">He 12:26</reference>, which quotes this passage; the apostle compares the heavier punishment which awaits the disobedient under the New Testament with that which met such under the Old Testament. At the establishment of the Sinaitic covenant, only the earth was shaken to introduce it, but now heaven and earth and all things are to be shaken, that is, along with prodigies in the world of nature, all kingdoms that stand in the way of Messiah's kingdom, "which cannot be shaken," are to be upturned (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.35">Da 2:35</reference>, 44; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>). <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">He 12:27</reference>, "Yet once more," favors English Version. Paul condenses together the two verses of Haggai (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Hag.2.21">Hag 2:21</reference>, 22), implying that it was one and the same shaking, of which the former verses of Haggai denote the beginning, the latter the end. The shaking began introductory to the first advent; it will be finished at the second. Concerning the former, compare <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.51">27:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.2">28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.2">Ac 2:2</reference>; 4:31; concerning the latter, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mt 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.20">Re 16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11">20:11</reference> [Bengel]. There is scarcely a prophecy of Messiah in the Old Testament which does not, to some extent at least, refer to His second coming [Sir Isaac Newton]. <reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Psa 68:8</reference> mentions the heavens dropping near the mountain (Sinai); but Haggai speaks of the whole created heavens: "Wait only a little while, though the promised event is not apparent yet; for soon will God change things for the better: do not stop short with these preludes and fix your eyes on the present state of the temple [Calvin]. God shook the heavens by the lightnings at Sinai; the earth, that it should give forth waters; the sea, that it should be divided asunder. In Christ's time God shook the heaven, when He spake from it; the earth, when it quaked; the sea, when He commanded the winds and waves [Grotius]. Cicero records at the time of Christ the silencing of the heathen oracles; and Dio, the fall of the idols in the Roman capitol. <div eID="gen24374" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12993"/><div sID="gen24375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12993"/><hi type="bold">7. shake--</hi>not convert; but cause that agitation which is to precede Messiah's coming as the healer of the nations' agitations. The previous shaking shall cause the yearning "desire" for the Prince of peace. Moore and others translate "the beauty," or "the desirable things (the precious gifts) of all nations shall come" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Is 60:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">61:6</reference>). He brings these objections to applying "the desire of all nations" to Messiah: (1) The Hebrew means the quality, not the thing desired, namely, its desirableness or beauty, But the abstract is often put for the concrete. So "a man of desires," that is, one desired or desirable (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Da 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">10:11</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">Da 10:3</reference>, Margin). (2) Messiah was not desired by all nations, but "a root out of a dry ground," having "no beauty that we should desire Him" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>). But what is implied is not that the nations definitely desired Him, but that He was the only one to satisfy the yearning desires which all felt unconsciously for a Saviour, shown in their painful rites and bloody sacrifices. Moreover, while the Jews as a nation desired Him not (to which people <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference> refers), the Gentiles, who are plainly pointed out by "all nations," accepted Him; and so to them He was peculiarly desirable. (3) The verb, "shall come," is plural, which requires the noun to be understood in the plural, whereas if Messiah be intended, the noun is singular. But when two nouns stand together, of which one is governed by the other, the verb agrees sometimes in number with the latter, though it really has the former as its nominative, that is, the Hebrew "come" is made in number to agree with "nations," though really agreeing with "the desire." Besides, Messiah may be described as realizing in Himself at His coming "the desires (the noun expressing collectively the plural) of all nations"; whence the verb is plural. So in <reference osisRef="Song.5.16">So 5:16</reference>, "He is altogether lovely," in the Hebrew the same word as here, "all desires," that is, altogether desirable, or the object of desires. (4) <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference>, "The silver is mine," &c.; accords with the translation, "the choice things of all nations" shall be brought in. But <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference> harmonizes quite as well with English Version of <reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>, as the note on eighth verse will show; see on <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference>. (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>) the Septuagint and Syriac versions agree with Moore's translation. But Vulgate confirms English Version. So also early Jewish Rabbis before Jerome's time. Plato [Alcibiades, 2] shows the yearning of the Gentiles after a spiritual deliverer: "It is therefore necessary," says Alcibiades on the subject of acceptable worship, "to wait until One teach us how we ought to behave towards the gods and men." Alcibiades replies, "When shall that time arrive, and who shall that Teacher be? For most glad would I be to see such a man." The "good tidings of great joy" were "to all people" (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.10">Lu 2:10</reference>). The Jews, and those in the adjoining nations instructed by them, looked for Shiloh to come unto whom the gathering of the people was to be, from Jacob's prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>). The early patriarchs, Job (Job 19:25-27; 33:23-26) and Abraham (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>), desired Him.<div eID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill this house with glory--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>). As the first temple was filled with the cloud of glory, the symbol of God (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.11">1Ki 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.14">2Ch 5:14</reference>), so this second temple was filled with the "glory" of God (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>) veiled in the flesh (as it were in the cloud) at Christ's first coming, when He entered it and performed miracles there (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.12-Matt.21.14">Mt 21:12-14</reference>); but that "glory" is to be revealed at His second coming, as this prophecy in its ulterior reference foretells (Mal 3:1). The Jews before the destruction of Jerusalem all expected Messiah would appear in the second temple. Since that time they invent various forced and false interpretations of such plain Messianic prophecies. <div eID="gen24376" type="x-p"/>

Is the seed yet in the barn?--</hi>implying, It is not. It has been already sown this month, and there are no more signs of its bearing a good crop, much less of its being safely stored in the barn, than there were in the past season, when there was such a failure; yet I promise to you from this day (emphatically marking by the repetition the connection of the blessing with the day of their obedience) a blessing in an abundant harvest. So also the vine, &c., which heretofore have borne little or nothing, shall be blessed with productiveness. Thus it will be made evident that the blessing is due to Me, not to nature. We may trust God's promise to bless us, though we see no visible sign of its fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Ha 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen24393" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13007"/><div sID="gen24395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13007"/><hi type="bold">21. to Zerubbabel--</hi>Perhaps Zerubbabel had asked as to the convulsions foretold (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>). This is the reply: The Jews had been led to fear that these convulsions would destroy their national existence. Zerubbabel, therefore, as their civil leader and representative is addressed, not Joshua, their religious leader. Messiah is the antitypical Zerubbabel, their national Representative and King, with whom God the Father makes the covenant wherein they, as identified with Him, are assured of safety in God's electing love (compare <reference osisRef="Hag.2.23">Hag 2:23</reference>, "will make thee as a signet"; "I have chosen thee").<div eID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake ... heavens--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>); violent political convulsions accompanied with physical prodigies (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mt 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">29</reference>). <div eID="gen24396" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13009"/><div sID="gen24398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13009"/><hi type="bold">23. take thee--</hi>under My protection and to promote thee and thy people to honor (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.70">Psa 78:70</reference>).<div eID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a signet--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.8.6">So 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jr 22:24</reference>). A ring with a seal on it; the legal representative of the owner; generally of precious stones and gold, &c., and much valued. Being worn on the finger, it was an object of constant regard. In all which points of view the theocratic people, and their representative, Zerubbabel the type, and Messiah his descendant the Antitype, are regarded by God. The safety of Israel to the end is guaranteed in Messiah, in whom God hath chosen them as His own (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">43:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1">44:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">49:3</reference>). So the spiritual Israel is sealed in their covenant head by His Spirit (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2Co 1:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>, 13, 14). All is ascribed, not to the merits of Zerubbabel, but to God's gratuitous choice. Christ is the "signet" on God's hand: always in the Father's presence, ever pleasing in his sight. The signet of an Eastern monarch was the sign of delegated authority; so Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Mt 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.23">23</reference>). <chapter eID="Hag.2"/><div eID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen24320" osisID="Hag" type="book"/>
